content: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is the official measure of inflation in the United Kingdom. Historically, the primary measure of inflation in the UK was the Retail Price Index (RPI), which was first calculated in the early 20th century. The RPI was initially developed to assess the impact of price changes on workers during the First World War. In October 1992, an explicit inflation target was introduced by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Norman Lamont, following the UK's withdrawal from the Exchange Rate Mechanism. At that time, the inflation target was based on the RPIX, a variation of the RPI that excluded mortgage interest payments. This exclusion was considered a more accurate reflection of the effectiveness of macroeconomic policy, as including mortgage payments could distort the measure when interest rates were adjusted to control inflation. Until 1997, interest rates in the UK were determined by the Treasury. However, after the New Labour government came to power in May 1997, control over interest rates was transferred to the Bank of England. The Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) was tasked with setting interest rates based on an inflation target established by the Chancellor. If inflation deviates by more than one percentage point from the target in any given month, the Governor of the Bank of England is required to write a formal letter to the Chancellor explaining the reasons for the deviation. Since 1996, the UK has also monitored a Consumer Price Index (CPI). In December 2003, the inflation target was shifted to one based on the CPI. As of May 2007, the inflation target was set at 3%, which includes mortgage interest payments. Both the CPI and the RPI are published monthly by the Office for National Statistics.
